hook.situation: A Korean colleague invites you for samgyeopsal tonight. You want to go, you probably can go — but you're not sure yet. In English you'd say 'I want to go,' 'I can go,' or 'I can't go.' Korean has three distinct grammar forms for these three meanings, and mixing them up sounds strange: saying 못 가고 싶어요 (a nonsensical blend) signals confusion between wanting and being able.
objectives: Use 고 싶어요 correctly to express what you want or desire to do
Use ㄹ/을 수 있어요 to say you can do something (ability or possibility)
Use 못 + verb to say you cannot do something — and know why 못 가해요 is wrong
hook.whyItMatters: These three patterns are the engine of polite Korean conversation. Koreans use them constantly to navigate invitations, menus, schedules, and apologies. Without them you can only say what you DO — you can't express what you want, what you're capable of, or what you have to decline. Master all three and you can have real adult conversations about your life.

grammarNotes.title: -고 싶어요 — saying what you want to do ("I want to…")
grammarNotes.func: Add -고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do. It's for your own wants; talking about what someone else wants uses -고 싶어 하다, which comes in a later chapter.

formTable.when: Verb stem ends in a vowel
Verb stem ends in a consonant (받침)
Past and negative go on 싶다, not the main verb
formTable.add: …고 싶었어요 (wanted to) / …고 싶지 않아요 (don't want to)
formTable.ex: 보다 → 보고 싶었어요 / 보고 싶지 않아요

examples.note: 마시다 ends in a vowel → 마시고 싶어요. The object keeps 을/를 (물을).

examples.en: I want to meet a friend today.
examples.note: 만나다 → 만나고 싶어요. It's your own wish, so plain -고 싶어요 is right.

examples.en: I want to watch a movie at home.
examples.note: 보다 → 보고 싶어요. The place where you do something takes 에서 (집에서).

examples.en: I wanted to study Korean more.
examples.note: Past tense goes on 싶다 (싶었어요), never on 공부하다.

keyPoint.label: Keep 을/를 on the thing you want
keyPoint.body: With -고 싶어요 the thing you want is still the object, so use 을/를: 밥을 먹고 싶어요 (I want to eat). You'll also hear 밥이 먹고 싶어요 in casual speech, but 밥을 먹고 싶어요 is the safe, standard choice for now.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 싶어요 links across the boundary and sounds like [시퍼요]; 먹고 tenses the ㄱ, so 먹고 싶어요 sounds like [먹꼬 시퍼요].

drill.instruction: Turn each verb into an "I want to…" sentence with -고 싶어요.
drill.model: 자다 → 자고 싶어요. (I want to sleep.)
items: 책을 읽다 → ____ (I want to read a book.)
집에 가다 → ____ (I want to go home.)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: "I want to be happy" tempts you to stick -고 싶어요 on 행복하다. But -고 싶어요 only goes on action verbs, not on adjectives (descriptive verbs). For a state, use 행복해지다 (become happy) or the wish pattern -으면 좋겠다.

grammarNotes.title: -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 / 없어요 — can and can't
grammarNotes.func: Add -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 to a verb stem for "can / be able to," and -(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 for "can't." Putting 못 right before the verb is a shorter, more everyday way to say "can't."

formTable.ex: 가다 → 갈 수 있어요 (can go) / 갈 수 없어요 (can't go)
먹다 → 먹을 수 있어요 (can eat) / 먹을 수 없어요 (can't eat)

formTable.add: stem + 수 있어요 (that ㄹ is the ending, add nothing)

formTable.ex: 먹다 → 못 먹어요 (can't eat) / 가다 → 못 가요 (can't go)

examples.ko: 저는 한국어를 조금 할 수 있어요.
examples.romanization: jeoneun hangugeoreul jogeum hal su isseoyo.
examples.en: I can speak a little Korean.
examples.note: 하다 ends in a vowel → 할 수 있어요.

examples.en: I can't go today because I don't have time.
examples.note: 못 + 가요 is the short, natural way to say "can't" about one situation.

examples.ko: 이 책은 너무 어려워서 읽을 수 없어요.
examples.romanization: i chaegeun neomu eoryeowoseo ilgeul su eopseoyo.
examples.en: This book is too hard, so I can't read it.
examples.note: 읽다 ends in a consonant → 읽을 수 없어요.
만들다 already ends in ㄹ, so add nothing → 만들 수 있어요.

keyPoint.label: 못 (can't) vs 안 (don't / won't)
keyPoint.body: Both sit right before the verb but mean different things. 못 = can't — you're unable, even if you'd like to (시간이 없어서 못 자요, I can't sleep because I have no time). 안 = a choice not to (피곤하지만 안 자요, I'm tired but I'm not going to sleep). So "can't eat" is 못 먹어요; "don't eat (by choice)" is 안 먹어요.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 수 있어요 links to [수 이써요]; 못 changes before the next sound — 못 가요 sounds like [몯까요] and 못 먹어요 like [몬머거요].

drill.instruction: Make a "can" sentence with -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요, then a "can't" sentence with 못.
drill.model: 가다 → 갈 수 있어요. / 못 가요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 수영을 안 할 수 있어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 저는 수영을 못 해요. / 수영을 할 수 없어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: For "I can't swim," learners try to negate 할 수 있어요 by adding 안. Korean doesn't do that — switch the whole phrase to 없어요 (할 수 없어요), or more naturally say 못 해요. Save 안 for choosing not to do something.

exampleSentence.en: I want to eat something that isn't spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 먹고 싶어요 — desire form; essential at Korean restaurants for dietary preferences
마시 + 고 싶어요 — the stem ends in a vowel so 고 attaches cleanly

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 내일 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go tomorrow.
exampleSentence.note: Two patterns in one sentence: 못 가요 (blocked today) vs 갈 수 있어요 (open tomorrow)

exampleSentence.en: I want to get better at Korean.
exampleSentence.note: 잘하 + 고 싶어요 — long-term aspiration; note that 못 for 하다 = 못 해요, NOT 못 하해요
말하다 → stem 말하 + ㄹ 수 있어요 → 말할 수 있어요; often used to express language ability

extendedVocabulary.english: to be able to eat / can eat

exampleSentence.ko: 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.note: 먹 (consonant ending stem) + 을 수 있어요 — consonant stems take 을 수, vowel stems take ㄹ 수

exampleSentence.ko: 이 음식은 너무 매워서 못 먹어요.
exampleSentence.en: This food is too spicy so I can't eat it.
exampleSentence.note: 맵다 is a ㅂ-irregular adjective: 매워서 (not 맵어서) — important for describing food limitations

exampleSentence.en: It's okay even if it's a little spicy.
exampleSentence.note: 괜찮아요 alone works as 'it's fine'; combined with 먹을 수 있어요 context it reassures the other person
알다 is ㄹ-irregular: 알 + 아요 = 알아요. For ability: 알 수 있어요 (stem already ends in ㄹ so no extra ㄹ added)

exampleSentence.en: Can you come to the party today?
exampleSentence.note: 오다 → stem 오 (vowel) → 올 수 있어요? A common social question — the ㄹ is added to the vowel stem

exampleSentence.en: I want to rest a bit today.
exampleSentence.note: 쉬 + 고 싶어요 — expressing the very human desire for rest; common in daily conversation

exampleSentence.en: Lately I'm busy so I can't exercise.
exampleSentence.note: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb: 못 + 해요 = 못 해요. The noun 운동 and 못 해요 can be separated: 운동 못 해요.

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘 시간이 있어요? 같이 밥 먹고 싶어요.
exampleSentence.en: Do you have time today? I want to eat together.
exampleSentence.note: 시간이 있어요 is the natural Korean way to say 'have time' — pairs perfectly with 고 싶어요 for invitations

exampleSentence.en: I'm too busy today so I can't go.
exampleSentence.note: 바쁘다 is ㅡ-irregular: 바빠서 (not 바쁘어서). Used constantly as a reason for 못 + verb

exampleSentence.en: What do you want to order?
exampleSentence.note: 주문하 + 고 싶어요 — essential restaurant phrase; 주문하다 is a 하다 verb

exampleSentence.ko: 아직 한국어를 다 이해할 수 없어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't understand all Korean yet.
exampleSentence.note: 이해하다 → 이해할 수 없어요 — a humble and accurate self-assessment for language learners

exampleSentence.ko: 오늘은 못 가요. 다음에 갈 수 있어요.
exampleSentence.en: I can't go today. I can go next time.
exampleSentence.note: 못 always goes BEFORE the verb. It's not a sentence ending — it's a pre-verb blocker. 못 가요, 못 먹어요, 못 마셔요.

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihye invites her coworker Minsu to dinner at a Korean BBQ restaurant

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 민수 씨, 오늘 저녁에 같이 밥 먹고 싶어요?
lines.romanization: Minsu ssi, oneul jeonyeoge gachi bap meokgo sipeoyo?
lines.en: Minsu, do you want to eat together this evening?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶어요? — a direct but polite desire question; the speaker checks whether Minsu wants the same thing

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 네, 먹고 싶어요! 어디에서 먹을 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Ne, meokgo sipeoyo! Eodieseo meogeul su isseoyo?
lines.en: Yes, I want to! Where can we eat?
lines.grammarNote: 먹고 싶어요 (desire) then 먹을 수 있어요 (possibility) — two different claims in two sentences. 먹 ends in a consonant, so 을 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 회사 식당이 좋아요. 지금 갈 수 있어요?
lines.romanization: Hoesa sikdangi joayo. Jigeum gal su isseoyo?
lines.en: The company cafeteria is good. Can you go now?
lines.grammarNote: 갈 수 있어요? — the open-door question. 가다 has a vowel stem 가, so ㄹ attaches directly: 갈 수 있어요.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 지금은 일이 많아요. 그래서 못 가요.
lines.romanization: Jigeumeun iri manayo. Geuraeseo mot gayo.
lines.en: Right now I have a lot of work. So I can't go.
lines.grammarNote: 못 가요 — the locked door: work blocks him. 못 goes directly before the verb, never inside it.

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.en: Then let's go in the evening. I'll wait.
lines.grammarNote: She answers a 못 with a workaround rather than a refusal — the normal Korean move

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.ko: 고마워요! 그런데 거기 밥이 매워요? 저는 못 먹어요.
lines.romanization: Gomawoyo! Geureonde geogi babi maewoyo? Jeoneun mot meogeoyo.
lines.en: Thanks! But is the food there spicy? I can't eat it.
lines.grammarNote: 못 먹어요 — a locked door for spicy food, i.e. a dietary limit rather than a lack of skill. 맵다 becomes 매워요 (ㅂ irregular).

lines.speaker: 지혜
lines.ko: 괜찮아요! 안 매운 밥도 주문할 수 있어요.
lines.romanization: Gwaenchanayo! An maeun bapdo jumunhal su isseoyo.
lines.en: It's fine! You can order non-spicy food too.
lines.grammarNote: 주문할 수 있어요 — the open door: the option exists. 주문하다 is a 하다 verb, so ㄹ attaches to 할.

lines.speaker: 민수
lines.en: Great! Then let's meet at the restaurant in the evening.
lines.grammarNote: No new grammar — but notice that want (먹고 싶어요), can (먹을 수 있어요) and can't (못 먹어요) all appeared naturally in one short exchange.

readingText.title: 단체 채팅방 — 이번 주말에 뭐 할 수 있어요? (Group Chat — What can everyone do this weekend?)
readingText.body:
지혜: 주말에 같이 한강에 가고 싶어요. 다 괜찮아요?
민수: 저도 가고 싶어요! 내일 시간이 있어요.
민준: 저는 오늘 일이 많아요. 그래서 못 가요.
민준: 그런데 내일은 갈 수 있어요.
지혜: 그럼 내일 가요! 거기에서 운동할 수 있어요?
민수: 네, 운동할 수 있어요. 밥도 먹을 수 있어요.
민준: 저는 커피를 못 마셔요. 물만 마셔요.
지혜: 괜찮아요! 물도 주문할 수 있어요.
민수: 내일 아침에 만나요. 그리고 같이 운동해요!
readingText.bodyTranslation:
Jihye: I want us to go to the Han River together this weekend. Is everyone okay with that?
Minsu: I want to go too! I have time tomorrow.
Minjun: I have a lot of work today. So I can't go.
Minjun: But tomorrow I can go.
Jihye: Then let's go tomorrow! Can we exercise there?
Minsu: Yes, we can exercise. We can eat there too.
Minjun: I can't drink coffee. I only drink water.
Jihye: That's fine! You can order water too.
Minsu: Let's meet tomorrow morning. And let's exercise together!

comprehensionQuestions.question: Why can't Minjun go today, and when can he go?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 오늘 일이 많아요. 그래서 못 가요 — too much work blocks him (못 = locked door). 내일은 갈 수 있어요 — tomorrow the door is open.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What can't Minjun drink, and what does he have instead?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 커피를 못 마셔요 (he can't drink coffee) — 물만 마셔요 (only water). Jihye reassures him: 물도 주문할 수 있어요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find every instance of 고 싶어요, -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요, and 못 in the text. For each one, identify which pattern it is and explain why that pattern is used instead of the others.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 고 싶어요 (desire): 가고 싶어요 ×2 — Jihye states her wish and Minsu shares it. -(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 (ability/possibility): 갈 수 있어요 (Minjun's door is open tomorrow), 운동할 수 있어요 ×2 (exercising there is possible), 먹을 수 있어요 (eating is possible — 먹 ends in a consonant, so 을 수 있어요), 주문할 수 있어요 (ordering water is possible). 못 (inability): 못 가요 (work blocks him today), 못 마셔요 (he cannot drink coffee at all). Wanting something and being able to do it are different claims, which is why 고 싶어요 and 수 있어요 never replace each other.

culturalNote.title: 못 해요 as the polite Korean refusal
culturalNote.body: In Korean social culture, saying you 'can't' do something (못 해요) is often more polite and face-saving than saying you 'don't want to' (싶지 않아요). If someone invites you somewhere you don't want to go, saying 오늘 못 가요 (I can't go today) is a softer decline than 가고 싶지 않아요 (I don't want to go), which can sound blunt or even rude. This is why Koreans sometimes use 못 해요 even when the real reason is lack of desire, not inability. When you start hearing 못 해요 in Korean conversations, know that it often carries the social function of a gentle 'no' — not necessarily a factual statement about impossibility.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 초밥을 먹___ 싶어요. (I want to eat sushi.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 고 싶어요 requires 고 between the verb stem and 싶어요. The stem of 먹다 is 먹, so: 먹고 싶어요. 을 would start the ability form (먹을 수 있어요), and 는 is a topic marker — neither makes sense here.

inlineExercises.prompt: 오늘 회의가 있어서 ___ 가요. (I can't go because I have a meeting today.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 expresses inability blocked by circumstances (the meeting). 안 가요 = 'I don't go / I won't go' (choice or habit, not inability). 고 싶지 않아요 = 'I don't want to go' (lack of desire). Only 못 captures 'I'm blocked — I can't.'

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장에서 틀린 것을 찾아보세요: '운동을 못 하해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 운동하다 is a 하다 verb. The 못 inability form for 하다 verbs is 못 해요 — NOT 못 하해요, which doubles the 하다 part. The noun and 못 해요 can be split naturally: 운동 못 해요.

inlineExercises.prompt: You want to say 'I can speak a little Korean.' Which is correct?
inlineExercises.explanation: 한국어로 marks the language used as the means of speaking, and 말할 수 있어요 = ability/capability (open door). Option A (말하고 싶어요) = 'I want to speak Korean' — desire, not ability. Option C (못 말해요) = 'I can't speak Korean' — the opposite of what you want to say.

inlineExercises.prompt: Translate: 'I want to rest today, but I can't.'
inlineExercises.correct: 오늘 쉬고 싶어요. 그런데 못 쉬어요.
inlineExercises.hint: You need two patterns: 쉬다 (to rest) with 고 싶어요 for desire, and 못 + verb for inability. The two parts contrast with 그런데 (but/however).
inlineExercises.explanation: -고 싶어요 expresses what you want to do. 못 쉬어요 says the situation blocks the action, not simply that you do not want to rest.

inlineExercises.prompt: 저는 매운 음식을 먹___ 수 있어요. (I can eat spicy food.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 먹다 has a consonant-ending stem (먹, ending in ㄱ). Consonant-ending stems take 을 수 있어요, not ㄹ 수 있어요. ㄹ 수 attaches to vowel-ending stems (가 → 갈 수, 오 → 올 수). 고 would start the desire form — not ability.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your Korean friend says '술 마시고 싶어요?' You can't drink alcohol. What's the most natural reply?
inlineExercises.explanation: 못 마셔요 is the most natural, socially smooth way to decline — it signals inability/circumstances rather than personal rejection, which is more polite in Korean culture. 마시고 싶지 않아요 (don't want to) sounds blunt. 마실 수 없어요 is grammatically fine but sounds formal/stiff in casual conversation. 못 마셔요 is the everyday go-to for dietary or health limitations.

inlineExercises.prompt: 한국어___ 조금 말할 수 있어요. (I can speak a little Korean.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 한국어 is what you speak, so it takes the object marker 를. 가 would make Korean the subject, which changes the sentence logic.
-고 싶어요 attaches to the verb stem to express desire. 가다 loses 다, then takes 고 싶어요: 가고 싶어요.
못 before the verb marks inability. 매운 음식 is the thing you cannot eat, so it takes 을.

bullets: MAGNET (고 싶어요): Verb stem + 고 싶어요 = desire, a pull toward an action. Always needs a verb — you can't attach it to a noun.
OPEN DOOR (ㄹ/을 수 있어요): Vowel stem + ㄹ 수 있어요 / Consonant stem + 을 수 있어요 = ability or possibility. The path is clear.
LOCKED DOOR (못 + verb): 못 goes BEFORE the regular verb form. Regular verbs use forms like 못 가요; 하다 verbs use 못 해요. Never make hybrids like 못 가해요 or 못 하해요.

writingTask.prompt: Reply to a friend planning the weekend: say one thing you want to do, one thing you can do, and one thing you can't.
writingTask.hint: Use V-고 싶어요 for wants, V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요 for can, and V-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 (or 못) for can't.
writingTask.model: 저는 영화를 보고 싶어요. 토요일에 갈 수 있어요. 그런데 일요일에는 못 가요.
writingTask.modelEn: I want to watch a movie. I can go on Saturday. But I can't go on Sunday.

canDo: Say what you want to do with V-고 싶어요 (가고 싶어요)
Say what you're able to do with V-(으)ㄹ 수 있어요
Say what you can't do with V-(으)ㄹ 수 없어요 or 못 + verb
Attach -(으)ㄹ correctly after a 받침 vs a vowel stem
